content:
There is some interest in general Eilenberg-Steenrod homology theories and what you can prove with them, so this thread is meant to help coordinate efforts in that direction.

Also in particular @Jacob Scharmberg has interest in this direction and applications thereof.

Thanks to @Vlad Tsyrklevich for the suggestion, I created a fresh repository following the guide. Interestingly, building a new project from scratch introduced a few minor errors into the lean files.

I do have some things to think about regarding idiomatic Lean programming which go a bit beyond the style guidelines.
This seems worth considering, as what might make sense to myself as the original author could very easily become twisted and convoluted to a new set of eyes, unless some mutually agreed upon universal standards are adhered to.

1) I make use of some select custom notation; in particular, (X, A)ₜₚ for a topological pair, as well as A ∩ᵣB for Subtype.val ⁻¹' A of type Set B (where we have X : Type* and A B : Set X). The latter custom notation is both a little bit obscuring for the type theoretic meaning, but is also a closer to the conventional mathematical notation used in the Mayer-Vietoris sequence, which would ideally align with and evoke the usual mathematical intuition.

2) In more complicated mathematical theories, you might have a large collection of hypotheses to work with, and passing them around as arguments to theorems will become unwieldy. A good approach seems to be to bundle these hypotheses into a structure in lean; then you could pass an instance of this structure as an argument. Even more complex - you might have a collection of hypotheses; definitions based on these hypotheses; and then more hypotheses based off of these definitions. Unfortunately, it seems you can't really use definitions within a structure, as these definitions are opaque and cannot be dsimped in the prover.

(This describes the situation for the Eilenberg-Steenrod axioms; and similarly the algebraic Mayer-Vietoris sequence; you have some axioms as hypotheses, as well as the hypotheses that the compositions are zero in the homology sequence; you then define the short complexes using the zero hypotheses; you add in more hypotheses that the short complexes are exact.)

The approach I took (mirroring somewhat the approach in Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Category.Basic) is to use a preliminary structure, then give the desired definitions based on this preliminary structure, then extend the preliminary structure. If anyone knows of some other lean files with similarly complex theories and structures that might be a helpful reference.

In any case, I do expect such situations to become more common as more and more complex theories get integrated into lean.

3) Also my thanks to @Joël Riou , his code for writing an exactness in an abelian category in terms of refinements allows for diagram chases exactly as one might hope in proving the long exact Mayer-Vietoris sequence.

4) Homology for a pair should probably be formulated in terms of a relation; it appears that writing H : ℤ → TopPair ⥤ Ab might run into issues as a dependent type.
